title: Query Optimisation: Plan Space Example
lead: Keep one shop query and change one execution decision at a time. Track the base reads, temporary writes, and work repeated by the join.
goals: Recalculate the cost after each plan refinement
Distinguish the effects of selection pushdown on the outer and inner inputs
Compare both choices of outer and inner join input
Include the cost of materializing a filtered inner input

sections.title: Count what is read, before counting what survives
sections.html:
Our shop wants customer names for qualifying orders. How can two plans that return the same names differ by thousands of page reads? Follow one original fixture throughout this lesson; it is separate from the Sailors/Reserves fixture in the official slides.

Orders occupies 600 pages; Customers occupies 200. A filter keeps 2% of Orders, or 12 pages if the surviving rows are packed together. A customer filter keeps 25%, or 50 packed pages. Both inputs are heap files: finding survivors requires reading the whole base file. We have B=8 buffer frames. Count page reads and temporary writes, exclude CPU and final-output writes, and pipeline a filtered outer input unless we explicitly materialize it.

Start with a page nested-loop join: take one outer page, scan the whole inner file for its matches, then take the next outer page. With Customers outside and Orders inside, the unfiltered plan reads 200 outer pages and repeats a 600-page inner scan 200 times.

Plan changeOuter acquisitionInner workTotal I/O
No early filter200200×600120,200
Filter Customers before joining20050×60030,200
Also filter Orders during every inner scan20050×60030,200

Why does the first filter help? The 200-page scan still happens, but only 50 packed outer pages reach the join, so Orders is scanned 50 times rather than 200. Why does the second filter not change this I/O total? Each inner repetition still reads all 600 pages to discover its matching rows. The filter reduces rows compared or emitted, not the pages visited by that heap scan.

The 12-page number describes a possible packed output, not an access path to those rows. It becomes a smaller file to reread only if we actually create and retain that file, or if a different access method can retrieve the survivors directly.

Can you replace 600 with 12 in the last row's inner cost?

No. That would pretend the filtered file already exists. In this plan it is recomputed from the 600-page heap for every outer page.

Key takeaway

Fewer rows after a filter do not necessarily mean fewer pages read. If every inner scan still reads the base table, the 12 pages of filtered Orders output do not replace the 600 pages that must be scanned.

Sources and teaching scope

Sources: PDF pages 3–13.

The worked examples and explanations are original teaching material. Optional extensions are labeled where they go beyond the core slides.

sections.title: Pay once to create an intermediate, then reuse it
sections.html:
Before adding a new algorithm, reverse the inputs. Filtered Orders now supplies 12 packed outer pages. Acquiring them still reads 600 base pages, but each outer page scans only the 200-page Customers file. Total: 600+12×200=3,000 I/Os. Inner and outer are roles in an execution algorithm; exchanging them does not change the inner-join answer.

Can the inner Customers scan be made smaller? Read its 200 pages once, filter, and write the 50 surviving pages into a temporary file. This is materialization: we pay an initial write so later scans can reuse a smaller result.

PhasePages chargedWhat exists afterward
Prepare filtered Customers200 reads + 50 writes50-page temporary inner file
Acquire filtered Orders600 reads12 packed outer pages, supplied as needed
Join12×50 readsSame qualifying joined rows
Total1,450CPU/final output excluded

Now compare the reverse materialized arrangement rather than assuming it must be worse. Use filtered Customers outside; read its 200-page heap once. Create a 12-page filtered Orders file by reading 600 and writing 12. Each of the 50 outer pages rereads those 12 pages. Total: 200+600+12+50×12=1,412.

The repeated reads are 600 in both arrangements: 12×50=50×12. The difference here is the temporary write, 50 versus 12. We have not claimed a universal “always put the smaller table inside” rule. The answer follows from this particular page-nested-loop model, acquisition costs, and materialization choices.

Why is 600+200+12×50=1,400 too low for the first arrangement?

It omits the 50 pages written to create the reusable Customers file. Reusing a file does not make its creation free.

Key takeaway

Separate base-table reads, temporary writes, and repeated temporary reads. Materialization reduces repeated-scan costs, but it is not free: the temporary result must also be written.

Sources and teaching scope

Sources: PDF pages 14–24.

The worked examples and explanations are original teaching material. Optional extensions are labeled where they go beyond the core slides.

sections.title: Memory and row width change the work that repeats
sections.html:
The page-nested-loop plan uses only one outer page at a time. With eight frames, reserve one for inner input and one for output; six remain for an outer block. The 50 filtered Customer pages form ceil(50/6)=9 blocks: eight full blocks and one two-page block. Every block scans the 12-page temporary Orders file once.

Read both base files for 800, write the Orders temporary for 12, then read it 9×12=108 times in page units. The block nested-loop total is 800+12+108=920 I/Os. The ceiling matters: a partial outer block still needs a full inner scan.

Next, keep only columns still needed. Suppose a filtered Orders row is 48 bytes but customer_id is eight bytes. The 12-page output shrinks to about 12×8/48=2 packed pages, ignoring page-overhead differences. Preserve duplicate keys: two orders must still produce two contributions. Those two pages fit in the six working frames. Read Orders once, retain the keys in RAM, then scan Customers once. No temporary write: 600+200=800 I/Os.

Give sorting its own ledger

Compare a fully materialized sort-merge plan on the original 12-page and 50-page filtered inputs, without that projection. Charge the 800 base reads once. With B=8, initial run creation writes 12+50 pages and makes ceil(12/8)=2 Orders runs, ceil(50/8)=7 Customers runs. Seven-way merging (B−1 inputs) finishes each in one merge pass.

Work after base scansOrdersCustomers
Initial run writes1250
Read and write one merge pass24100
Read sorted input for join1250

Total: 800+12+24+12+50+100+50=1,048. Final join output writes and CPU remain excluded; we do not fuse final sorting with joining in this candidate.

Reduce B to 7. Customers starts with ceil(50/7)=8 runs, but fan-in is only 6. Its run counts become 8→2→1, requiring two merge passes. Its overhead after the base scan is now 50+2×50×2=250; Orders still adds 12+24=36. Joining reads another 62, so total becomes 800+36+250+62=1,148. A memory threshold changes the number of whole passes, not just a small fraction of cost.

Sources and teaching scope

Sources: PDF pages 25–42; Source PDF · physical pages 25, 26, 27, 28, 29.

sections.title: Exercise: compare plans under the same access assumptions
sections.html:
Change the fixture explicitly: an available clustered access path now retrieves 1,200 qualifying Orders rows from 12 pages for 12 I/Os. Each row probes a unique Customers key. The Customers index is already in RAM; each successful probe costs one data-page read. Compare indexed nested loops against retaining the two-page projected key list and scanning the 200-page Customers file.

Calculate both complete candidates

Indexed nested loops makes one probe per row, not per outer page. Its cost is 12+1,200×1=1,212 I/Os. Retaining projected keys in RAM costs the same 12 to acquire Orders, then 200 to scan Customers, totaling 212. Keep duplicate keys so each qualifying order contributes an output row.

The earlier 800-I/O plan used heap access to Orders. Comparing 1,212 directly with 800 would mix access assumptions. Give both new candidates the same 12-page clustered access before judging the join strategy.

Try a second case yourself: only 30 outer rows survive and fit on one clustered page, with the same Customers assumptions.

Check the reversal

Indexed nested loops costs 1+30=31; retaining keys and scanning Customers costs 1+200=201. Now probes win. An index's presence alone did not decide the outcome: the number of outer rows determines how often its lookup cost repeats.

Use the join-cost lab to vary outer pages and buffer frames. Before accepting a displayed total, write the assumptions beside it: base acquisition, retained temporary size, number of repeated scans, row count for probes, and whether final output or sorting is charged.

Sources and teaching scope

quiz.question: Does filtering an inner heap from 600 pages to 12 output pages automatically reduce each scan to 12 I/Os?
options: No, if each scan still reads the 600-page heap
It depends only on the number of SELECT columns
quiz.explanation: Output size and the number of input pages that must be read are different quantities.
